headline: Oxford compressor malfunction released more than 35 million cubic feet of gas, report says
dek: A July emergency shutdown at Enbridge's Oxford station sent a large natural-gas release into the air while residents in three Connecticut towns heard a jet-engine-like roar; regulators have not said whether air-quality rules were violated.
body: Residents in Oxford, Middlebury and Naugatuck were awakened by a jet-engine-like roar in the early hours of July 12. A new Connecticut Public report, republished by CT Mirror on Sept. 30, says the sound came from two equipment failures at Enbridge's Oxford natural-gas compressor station and that the episode released more than 35 million cubic feet of gas in less than an hour.

The event is receiving fresh attention because the federal incident record describes it as the largest natural-gas release reported to the government in Connecticut in the past decade, according to Connecticut Public's review of Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration data. The report places it among the top 10% of releases recorded nationwide over that period. Connecticut Public compared the volume with 2024 U.S. Energy Information Administration consumption data, available at https://www.eia.gov/dnav/ng/ng_sum_lsum_dcu_sct_a.htm, and estimated it was roughly equivalent to a year's gas use for 450 Connecticut homes. That comparison is an estimate, not a measurement of how much gas any nearby household used.

The reported sequence began at about 12:47 a.m., when a loose connection on a newly installed emergency pull switch triggered a shutdown. The shutdown system is designed to stop compressor units, isolate the station from the pipeline and vent gas remaining in the equipment. A valve that was supposed to complete that isolation did not close fully, however, allowing gas to continue moving from the pipeline through discharge pipes and into the atmosphere. Personnel manually closed the valve at about 1:40 a.m., after approximately 53 minutes, the federal incident data showed as described by Connecticut Public.

A compressor station raises gas pressure so it can travel through a long pipeline system. Connecticut DEEP's permit materials identify the Oxford facility as part of Algonquin Gas Transmission, a roughly 1,100-mile network serving New England, New York and New Jersey. The agency's permit document is available at https://portal.ct.gov/-/media/deep/air/permits/titlev/algonquin_oxford/p144-0021.pdf. The distance matters locally: the station's equipment is tied to a regional energy system, but its emergency release was heard by people living miles away. The federal reporting system explains at https://www.phmsa.dot.gov/data-and-statistics/pipeline/distribution-transmission-gathering-lng-and-liquid-accident-and-incident-data that operators submit information about incident timing, location, facility details, gas released and causes of failure.

Enbridge told Connecticut Public that the station experienced an unplanned outage and that there was no threat to public safety. Residents interviewed for the report said they were not told how much gas had been released or what would be done to prevent a repeat. The available reporting does not establish that anyone was injured, and it does not independently determine whether the release violated an air-quality law. Those distinctions matter: a loud emergency release, a reported volume and a regulatory violation are separate questions.

Environmental-health experts quoted by Connecticut Public said a large natural-gas release can raise concerns about methane, combustible gas and other compounds, including possible short-term irritation, headache, nausea or dizziness at sufficiently high concentrations. Those comments describe potential effects, not confirmed diagnoses among Oxford-area residents. Connecticut's Department of Energy and Environmental Protection also said the operator had not submitted a Clean Air Act deviation report related to the episode as of the report's publication. The report says DEEP does not directly regulate blowdowns and pointed to federal pipeline oversight; the Public Utilities Regulatory Authority declined to comment because the matter could come before it for adjudication.

The next phase is therefore about documentation as much as the original malfunction. PHMSA says pipeline operators must report qualifying incidents within 30 days and that the records are used for safety analysis and inspection planning; its incident-reporting guidance is at https://www.phmsa.dot.gov/incident-reporting. The state PURA describes its gas-pipeline-safety role at https://portal.ct.gov/pura/gas-pipeline-safety/gas-pipeline-safety. The central unanswered questions are whether the emergency-shutdown equipment has been repaired or redesigned, whether any state or federal review will assess the blowdown under air rules, and how nearby residents will be notified if a similar release occurs.

For communities around compressor stations, the episode is a reminder that pipeline safety is not only an engineering issue. Residents need timely information about what they heard, what was released and whether officials found a continuing hazard. Enbridge's statement addresses immediate public-safety risk, while the federal incident record and the state agencies' positions leave longer-term accountability unresolved. Until those records and reviews are made clearer, the July event remains both a documented equipment failure and an open question about public communication.
author: NorthEast News Desk
seoTitle: Oxford compressor station gas release in Connecticut
seoDescription: A July malfunction at an Oxford, Connecticut, compressor station released more than 35 million cubic feet of natural gas, according to federal incident data reviewed by Connecticut Public.
